challenges.name: sessions-vs-tokens-quiz
challenges.title: What logout and a password reset really revoke
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from CodeDev sign-in: a fake-clock timeline of the new 15-minute access token after a password reset, and a server-side session logout handler with the sessions table after logout.

questions.question:
The new design: access tokens live 15 minutes and are verified locally (signature and exp only); refresh tokens are opaque, hashed in auth.refresh_tokens and checked against the table on every refresh. An attacker copied both tokens of learner u_1042 right after the 14:00 refresh. Fake-clock test log:

14:00:00 refresh -> new access token (iat 14:00:00, exp 14:15:00) + new refresh token
14:05:41 POST /auth/password-reset 204
         UPDATE auth.refresh_tokens SET revoked_at = now() WHERE user_id = 'u_1042' AND revoked_at IS NULL  -- 1 row
14:09:00 GET /me/progress (access token from 14:00) -> 200
14:10:00 POST /auth/refresh (refresh token from 14:00) -> 401 refresh_token_revoked
14:15:00 GET /me/progress (access token from 14:00) -> 401 token_expired

Statement: "The attacker can call the API with the copied access token until 14:15 at the latest, and cannot obtain a new access token after the reset."
questions.explanation: True. The access token is verified without a lookup, so the reset cannot touch it: it keeps working until its exp at 14:15, as the 200 at 14:09 shows. Getting a new one requires the refresh token, and the refresh endpoint checks auth.refresh_tokens, where the reset set revoked_at on the only active row, hence the 401 at 14:10. That bounded window (at most the access token lifetime) is the whole point of the 15-minute access token plus refresh token design. The common misconception is that a password reset signs out a JWT immediately; it only stops the next refresh, so the access token lifetime is the length of the window you accept.

False. clearCookie only tells this one browser to forget its copy. The session row 9f1c…e2 is still in admin.sessions with an expiry in the future, so any request that presents the old sid value, from curl or another browser, still finds a valid session until 21:00. Logout in a server-side session design must delete or revoke the row (DELETE FROM admin.sessions WHERE id = $1) and then clear the cookie; the OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet asks for the session to be invalidated on the server side. The misconception is that logout is something the client does: the server's state decides whether a credential works.
